Content:
Consider the polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}] below. How can we construct a polygon with the same shape as [MATH: \mathcal{P}] but whose side lengths are twice those of [MATH: \mathcal{P}?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6e0300c61f8ee4abf55058d40b3d51df]

Content:
First, we pick a random point [MATH: O] in the plane. Then, we draw three line segments that connect the point [MATH: O] with the vertices of our polygon.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/68014d0474c773ec79e1bc3bca2fd413]

Content:
Next, we increase the length of each segment by a factor of [MATH: 2.] Notice that each segment should have [MATH: O] as one of its endpoints.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/45c1e442529f64fd543b56c934cf6346]

Content:
Finally, we connect the endpoints of the enlarged segments using edges, and we obtain a new polygon [MATH: \mathcal P'.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e5c494e7b06c4a6ed895b7dfc8450f61]

Content:
The new polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}'] has the same shape as [MATH: \mathcal{P},] but each side has a length that is twice as long as the corresponding side length of [MATH: \mathcal P.]

Content:
The transformation we just applied is called an enlargement with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: k=2.]

Content:
For an enlargement, we must have [MATH: |k| > 1.] We can split this into two cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: k] is positive, then the original polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] and its image [MATH: \mathcal P'] lie in the same direction from [MATH: O.]
- If [MATH: k] is negative, then the original polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] and its image [MATH: \mathcal P'] lie in the opposite directions from [MATH: O.]

Content:
We will first explore the case where [MATH: k] is positive. The cases when [MATH: k] is negative will be dealt with toward the end of the lesson.

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that, in the diagram above, we have that

[MATH: \dfrac{B'C'}{BC} = \dfrac52 ,]

and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor [MATH: k] is [MATH: |k|=\dfrac52.]

Since the points [MATH: B] and [MATH: B'] lie in the same direction from [MATH: O], the scale factor [MATH: k] is positive. Therefore, [MATH: k=\dfrac52.]

So far, we have only considered dilations where the scale factor [MATH: k > 0.] But what happens if the scale factor is negative?

For example, let's dilate the polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] below using a scale factor [MATH: k=-2.]

As usual, we draw three line segments that connect the point [MATH: O] with the vertices of our polygon.

Graphic:

Content:
As always, our segments have one common endpoint, the point [MATH: O.]

Content:
Next, we flip the three line segments over the point [MATH: O] and increase the length of each segment by a factor of [MATH: |{-2}|=2,] keeping the point [MATH: O] fixed.

Graphic:

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}] below. How can we construct a polygon with the same shape as [MATH: \mathcal{P}] but whose side lengths are twice those of [MATH: \mathcal{P}?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6e0300c61f8ee4abf55058d40b3d51df]

Content:
First, we pick a random point [MATH: O] in the plane. Then, we draw three line segments that connect the point [MATH: O] with the vertices of our polygon.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/68014d0474c773ec79e1bc3bca2fd413]

Content:
Next, we increase the length of each segment by a factor of [MATH: 2.] Notice that each segment should have [MATH: O] as one of its endpoints.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/45c1e442529f64fd543b56c934cf6346]

Content:
Finally, we connect the endpoints of the enlarged segments using edges, and we obtain a new polygon [MATH: \mathcal P'.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e5c494e7b06c4a6ed895b7dfc8450f61]

Content:
The new polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}'] has the same shape as [MATH: \mathcal{P},] but each side has a length that is twice as long as the corresponding side length of [MATH: \mathcal P.]

Content:
The transformation we just applied is called an enlargement with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: k=2.]

Content:
For an enlargement, we must have [MATH: |k| > 1.] We can split this into two cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: k] is positive, then the original polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] and its image [MATH: \mathcal P'] lie in the same direction from [MATH: O.]
- If [MATH: k] is negative, then the original polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] and its image [MATH: \mathcal P'] lie in the opposite directions from [MATH: O.]

Content:
We will first explore the case where [MATH: k] is positive. The cases when [MATH: k] is negative will be dealt with toward the end of the lesson.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Scale Factor of an Enlargement

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/b0c3ef0b53be9b02a08ec73fe5d84112]

The polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}'] is the image of the polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}] under an enlargement with center [MATH: O.] What is the scale factor of the enlargement?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:

Notice that, in the diagram above, we have that

[MATH: \dfrac{B'C'}{BC} = \dfrac52 ,]

and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor [MATH: k] is [MATH: |k|=\dfrac52.]

Since the points [MATH: B] and [MATH: B'] lie in the same direction from [MATH: O], the scale factor [MATH: k] is positive. Therefore, [MATH: k=\dfrac52.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Contractions

Content:
Notice that point [MATH: O] is a common endpoint to all three segments.

Content:

Content:

Graphic:

Content:
The new polygon [MATH: \mathcal{P}'] has the same shape as [MATH: \mathcal{P},] but its lengths are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] times those of [MATH: \mathcal P.]

Content:
The transformation we just applied is called a contraction with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: k=\dfrac 12.]

Content:
For a contraction, we must have [MATH: |k| < 1.] Again, we can split this into two cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: k] is positive, then the original polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] and its image [MATH: \mathcal P'] lie in the same direction from [MATH: O.]
- If [MATH: k] is negative, then the original polygon [MATH: \mathcal P] and its image [MATH: \mathcal P'] lie in the opposite directions from [MATH: O.]

Content:
Again, we'll first concern ourselves with positive [MATH: k] only.

Content:
Finally, we use the term dilation to refer to both enlargements and contractions.
